concepts.title: Meaning, Features and Importance of Directing

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meaning, Features and Importance of Directing' refers to.
questions.a: The managerial function that steers people at work through instructions, guidance, counselling, motivation and leadership so that the organisation's objectives are actually pursued; it is the spark that puts plans to work and runs at every level for as long as the organisation lives.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meaning, Features and Importance of Directing'.
questions.a: Four marks: it initiates action, exists wherever superior-subordinate relations exist, never stops, and flows down the hierarchy; its worth lies in starting action, joining individual efforts, drawing out potential, easing change and keeping the organisation balanced.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meaning, Features and Importance of Directing' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: lebs107.txt lines 84-254 (Meaning; characteristics i-iv; importance i-v))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Principles of Directing' refers to.
questions.a: Eight guides for effective direction: draw the maximum contribution from each person, harmonise individual and organisational aims, keep one boss per person, pick techniques that fit the subordinate, communicate clearly with feedback, use informal groups wisely, lead well, and always follow up on orders given.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Principles of Directing'.
questions.a: Match the principle to the case -- rewards suiting each worker show appropriateness of technique; a manager reviewing orders shows follow through.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Principles of Directing' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 2.1 (source: lebs107.txt lines 255-368 (Principles i-viii))

concepts.title: Supervision as an Element of Directing

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Supervision as an Element of Directing' refers to.
questions.a: The overseeing of subordinates' work with guidance and instruction so that resources are used well and targets are met; it is both an element every manager performs and the job title of the operative-level manager standing directly above the workers.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Supervision as an Element of Directing'.
questions.a: The supervisor is the workers' guide, friend and philosopher and the link carrying management's ideas down and workers' problems up.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Supervision as an Element of Directing' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 3.1 (source: lebs107.txt lines 400-537 (Supervision, two meanings; importance i-vii))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Motivation -- Concept, Features and Process' refers to.
questions.a: The process of stirring subordinates to act in the desired way so that organisational goals are served; it begins with an inner state called a motive, works through stimulation called motivation, and applies tools called motivators such as pay, praise or promotion.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Motivation -- Concept, Features and Process'.
questions.a: It is an internal feeling producing goal-directed behaviour, may be positive or negative, and affects different people differently; the chain runs from unsatisfied need to tension, drives, search behaviour, satisfaction and relief of tension.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Motivation -- Concept, Features and Process' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 4.1 (source: lebs107.txt lines 538-707 (motive, motivation, motivators; features i-iv; motivation process and Ramu example))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Maslow's Need Hierarchy Theory' refers to.
questions.a: Abraham Maslow's ladder of five human needs, rising from basic physiological needs such as food and shelter, through safety, belonging and esteem, to self-actualisation, the drive to become all one is capable of becoming.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Maslow's Need Hierarchy Theory'.
questions.a: Assumptions to cite: behaviour flows from needs, needs stand in a hierarchy, a satisfied need no longer motivates, and the next level pulls only after the lower one is met -- basic salary serves the bottom rung, pension plans the second, friendship the third, status the fourth, growth the top.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Maslow's Need Hierarchy Theory' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 4.2 (source: lebs107.txt lines 828-940 (Maslow's theory: five needs i-v, assumptions i-iv, criticism))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Financial Incentives' refers to.
questions.a: Motivators payable in money or measurable in money: pay and allowances, productivity-linked wages, bonus, a share in profits, stock options that make employees co-owners, retirement benefits such as provident fund and pension, and perquisites like housing, car allowance or medical aid.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Financial Incentives'.
questions.a: Money buys daily needs plus social standing, so it stays the most direct incentive; stock options go further by creating a feeling of ownership.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Financial Incentives' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 4.3 (source: lebs107.txt lines 941-1094 (Financial incentives i-vii))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Non-Financial Incentives' refers to.
questions.a: Motivators aimed at psychological, social and emotional needs rather than the purse: status, a supportive organisational climate, career advancement opportunities, enriched jobs with autonomy and challenge, recognition programmes, job security, employee participation in decisions, and empowerment with greater autonomy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Non-Financial Incentives'.
questions.a: Money alone cannot satisfy every need; a promotion may raise pay but its real pull is elevation, status and authority -- the psychological over the monetary.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Non-Financial Incentives' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 4.4 (source: lebs107.txt lines 1095-1251 (Non-financial incentives i-viii))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Leadership -- Meaning, Features and Importance' refers to.
questions.a: The art of influencing people so that they strive willingly toward group goals; it rests on the ability to build good interpersonal relations with followers and to draw their best contribution without coercion.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Leadership -- Meaning, Features and Importance'.
questions.a: Its features: the power to influence, a change agent for behaviour, interpersonal between leader and followers, aimed at common goals, and continuous; its worth shows in positive contribution, need fulfilment, smoother change, conflict handling and successor building -- and followers, by accepting leadership, co-create the leader.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Leadership -- Meaning, Features and Importance' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.1 (source: lebs107.txt lines 1252-1387 (definitions box; features i-v; importance i-v))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Leadership Styles' refers to.
questions.a: Three patterns of using authority: the autocratic leader commands and expects obedience with one-way communication, the democratic leader consults subordinates before deciding, and the laissez-faire leader leaves followers free to set their own objectives, stepping in only to support and supply information.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Leadership Styles'.
questions.a: Autocracy buys speed and discipline on the shop floor; democracy buys commitment through participation; free-rein buys creativity from capable teams -- a leader may blend styles as the situation demands.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Leadership Styles' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.2 (source: lebs107.txt lines 1388-1487 (Autocratic, Democratic, Laissez faire styles))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Communication Process and Its Elements' refers to.
questions.a: The exchange of ideas, facts and feelings between people so that a common understanding emerges; the chain runs from sender through encoding, media of transmission and decoding to receiver, with feedback closing the loop and noise threatening every link.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Communication Process and Its Elements'.
questions.a: Encoding turns ideas into words or gestures, decoding reverses the process at the receiver; noise is any obstruction -- bad phone lines, ambiguous symbols, an inattentive listener, prejudices, mismatched body language.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Communication Process and Its Elements' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.1 (source: lebs107.txt lines 1488-1601 (definitions; elements of communication process i-viii; noise examples))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Importance of Communication' refers to.
questions.a: The reasons the function is central to managing: it underpins coordination, keeps the enterprise working smoothly, supplies the information behind decisions, raises managerial efficiency, builds cooperation and industrial peace, grounds leadership, and lifts morale and motivation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Importance of Communication'.
questions.a: A manager spends most of the working day communicating; when communication stops, organised activity itself ceases.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Importance of Communication' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.2 (source: lebs107.txt lines 1573-1725 (Importance of Communication i-vii))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Formal and Informal Communication' refers to.
questions.a: Official messages move through the channels drawn on the organisation chart -- vertical, upward or downward, and horizontal between sister divisions -- over networks like the single chain, wheel, circular, free flow and inverted V; unofficial exchange, the grapevine, ignores these lines entirely and spreads in single strand, gossip, probability or cluster patterns.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Formal and Informal Communication'.
questions.a: Grapevine talk travels fast, distorts easily and hides its source, yet a wise manager taps it to sound out reactions -- the cluster network is the most common.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Formal and Informal Communication' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.3 (source: lebs107.txt lines 1726-1907 (Formal and informal communication; networks; grapevine networks))

concepts.title: Barriers to Communication and Their Remedies

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Barriers to Communication and Their Remedies' refers to.
questions.a: Four families of obstruction: semantic barriers of badly expressed or wrongly translated words, technical jargon and ambiguous symbols; psychological barriers like premature evaluation, inattention, loss in transmission and distrust; organisational barriers from rigid rules, status distance and layered structures; and personal barriers such as fear of challenge or unwillingness to speak up.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Barriers to Communication and Their Remedies'.
questions.a: Remedies mirror the barriers -- clarify ideas first, suit the receiver's level, consult before sending, watch language and tone, convey useful content, ensure feedback, think of the future, follow up, and listen well.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Barriers to Communication and Their Remedies' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.4 (source: lebs107.txt lines 1893-2375 (Barriers: semantic, psychological, organisational, personal; improving communication effectiveness i-ix))
